title: Capturing the daylight dividend in buildings: why and how?
review_question: To review the literature on daylighting, its benefits ('why') and design principles ('how') for buildings, and to identify future research directions.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting (design of buildings to use light from the Sun)
findings.quote: Energy is not saved by daylighting; energy is saved by dimming down or switching off electric lights that are not needed because of daylight.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting apertures with proper sun control
findings.consequent: Air conditioning energy requirements (due to reduced internal cooling load from lights)
findings.quote: Daylighting often reduces air conditioning energy requirements as well because the internal cooling load from the lights is reduced.

findings.antecedent: Reduced lighting and cooling loads from daylighting
findings.quote: The combined savings from reduced lighting and cooling loads can be substantial because electric lighting can account for 25-40% of a commercial building's energy requirements.

findings.antecedent: Electric energy savings from daylighting
findings.consequent: Power plant emissions (acid rain, air pollution, global warming)
findings.quote: Electric energy savings also result in fewer power plant emissions that contribute to acid rain, air pollution, and global warming.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting
findings.quote: the strongest economic argument for daylighting may be the worker's improved productivity, increased job satisfaction, or reduced absenteeism

findings.antecedent: Daylight
findings.consequent: Ability to continue working on some tasks during power outages
findings.quote: Daylight allows people to continue working on some tasks during power outages.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting / Windows
findings.consequent: Perceived health, indoor environmental quality, productivity, preference
findings.quote: People care about so-called green buildings and associate daylighting with healthy buildings and indoor environmental quality. They have a strong preference for windows in their offices [2,3] and believe windows improve their productivity.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting
findings.quote: Aesthetically, daylight offers features that electric lighting systems do not. Most importantly, building occupants value the view that windows provide.

findings.antecedent: More light (from daylighting)
findings.quote: It is well understood that more light makes it easier to see visual tasks. More light will improve performance, although with rapidly decreasing impact once one is above the recommended level.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting
findings.quote: A great benefit of daylight is that it allows our buildings to be lit at higher levels than with electric lighting alone.

findings.antecedent: Daylighting
findings.quote: Daylight also provides a broad electromagnetic spectrum with excellent color rendering

findings.antecedent: Daylight levels (typical of daylight, order of magnitude above normal electric lighting)
findings.quote: Experimental work indicates that suppression of melatonin... is influenced by exposure to light levels typical of daylight... Thus, daylight provides the right quantity and quality of light to trigger the circadian systems.

findings.antecedent: Disruption of intensity, duration, or time of exposure to light (lack of regular daylight exposure)
findings.consequent: Fatigue, mood shifts (Seasonal Affective Disorder), reduced performance
findings.quote: Disruption of the intensity, duration, or time of exposure to light, may indeed contribute to fatigue, mood shifts such as Seasonal Affective Disorder, and reduced performance

findings.antecedent: Skylights
findings.quote: A 1999 study, for example, reports a correlation between skylights and higher retail sales [7]. They concluded that the skylights account for about a 40% increase in sales. This conclusion may or may not be accurate.

findings.antecedent: Improper daylighting design (excessive solar heat gain, glare, material degradation, AV interference, privacy issues)
findings.consequent: Occupant discomfort, impeded vision, excessive energy demand, material degradation, privacy issues
findings.quote: Done improperly, it impedes vision, causes discomfort, and demands excessive energy.

findings.antecedent: Building configuration (most floor area within daylight zone, ~5m from window wall or top floor with skylights)
findings.quote: Configure the building so that most of the floor area occupied by people is within the daylight zone. The typical daylight zone is about 5 m deep from the window wall or the top floor of a building with skylights.

findings.antecedent: Building elongated along an east-west axis
findings.consequent: Excessive solar heat gain in summer, north daylighting apertures (or south in southern hemisphere)
findings.quote: Elongate a building along an east-west axis to avoid excessive solar heat gain in the summer months and to maximize north daylighting apertures (south apertures in the southern hemisphere).

findings.antecedent: Critical visual tasks located near building's perimeter
findings.quote: Locate critical visual tasks near the building's perimeter.

findings.antecedent: High windows on the wall (light brought in high)
findings.quote: Bring the light in high. Windows higher on the wall will allow the light to penetrate further into the space.

findings.antecedent: Bilateral lighting (daylight from more than one side of a space)
findings.consequent: Uniformity and balanced brightness within room
findings.quote: Admit daylight from more than one side of a space where possible. Bilateral lighting, for example, increases uniformity and balances the brightness within the room.

findings.antecedent: Controlled direct sun (bounced off horizontal elements, window blinds, non-specular surfaces)
findings.quote: Control the direct sun. Bounce the direct sun off horizontal elements, window blinds, and other non-specular surfaces to distribute and diffuse the light.

findings.antecedent: Light-colored interior surfaces
findings.consequent: Luminance contrast between windows and surrounding surfaces, visual comfort
findings.quote: Use light-colored interior surfaces. Light surfaces reduce the luminance contrast between the windows and surrounding surfaces, increasing visual comfort.

findings.antecedent: Workstations and computer screens located perpendicular to windows
findings.consequent: Reflected glare in screens, visual discomfort
findings.quote: Locate workstations and computer screens perpendicular to the windows to reduce reflected glare in the screens or visual discomfort.

findings.antecedent: Light shelves (horizontal projections dividing south windows into lower view and upper clerestory sections)
findings.quote: Light shelves... reflect sunlight onto a light-colored ceiling, increasing the daylight zone by a few meters under sunny conditions.

findings.antecedent: High windows and high ceilings
findings.quote: Buildings with high windows and high ceilings have extended daylight zones as well.

findings.antecedent: Horizontal blinds adjusted to direct sunlight to the ceiling
findings.consequent: Depth of daylight penetration, view maintenance, excessive brightness on work tasks
findings.quote: Horizontal blinds adjusted to direct sunlight to the ceiling also increase the depth of daylight penetration, maintain a view, and reduce excessive brightness on work tasks.

findings.antecedent: Window blinds or shades (pulled to eliminate direct sun and not readjusted)
findings.consequent: Available daylight on east, south, and west facades
findings.quote: Window blinds can easily occlude more than half of the available daylight on the east, south, and west facades [11].

findings.antecedent: Prismatic glass blocks / Holographic films
findings.consequent: Direction of sun towards ceiling deeper in space
findings.quote: Prismatic glass blocks have been used in buildings to direct some of the sun towards the ceiling. More recently, holographic films have been proposed to direct sunlight to the ceiling deeper in the space, but currently these films are not sufficiently effective to justify the investment.

findings.antecedent: Low transmission glazing (to control overheating and reduce mechanical system size)
findings.consequent: Occupant acceptability, perceived dimness, addition of electric light, energy savings from daylight
findings.quote: Glass with very low transmission, however, may be unacceptable to occupants [12]. If the resulting interior space appears dim, occupants may add more electric light, further reducing any energy savings from daylight.

findings.antecedent: Certain tints of glass (e.g., bronze vs. blue-tinted with same transmittance)
findings.quote: Bronze glass, for example, can make a view appear significantly brighter than the same view seen through blue-tinted glass with the same transmittance. People will feel the space is brighter, although there is no improvement in visual task performance [13].

findings.antecedent: Skylights, roof monitors, clerestory windows, translucent roofs (for top floor)
findings.consequent: Light for areas beyond perimeter zone
findings.quote: For the top floor, skylights, roof monitors, clerestory windows, and translucent roofs are used to light areas beyond the perimeter zone.

findings.antecedent: Vertical spaces within building's footprint exposed to sky (atria, light wells)
findings.consequent: Daylighting for deep, multi-story buildings (internal perimeter)
findings.quote: One approach is to extend the perimeter zone by vertical spaces within the building's footprint that are exposed to the sky. These spaces create an internal perimeter that can be daylit.

findings.antecedent: Beam daylighting systems (optics, fiber optics)
findings.quote: Because of the expense and maintenance of the collection system, the optical losses within the conveying system, and building code issues [16], these systems are not economically viable for general-purpose lighting.

findings.antecedent: Lighting controls (for daylighting)
findings.quote: Controls are the key to energy savings when using daylighting [17].

findings.antecedent: Switch sticker reminders + management encouragement
findings.consequent: Light usage, cost-effectiveness (compared to automatic controls)
findings.quote: Switch sticker reminders to turn off lights, coupled with encouragement from management, may be more cost effective than automatic daylight control systems [18].

findings.antecedent: Manual dimming (in private offices)
findings.quote: Manual dimming can also be an effective energy-savings strategy in private offices [19].

findings.antecedent: Luminaires clearly within occupants' own work area (in open plan/multi-person spaces)
findings.consequent: Occupants' inclination to turn off lights
findings.quote: In open plan and other multi-person spaces, occupants are more inclined to turn off lights if the luminaires are clearly within their own work area.

findings.antecedent: Luminaires closest to window walls controlled separately
findings.consequent: Energy savings (by switching/dimming when sufficient daylight)
findings.quote: The row of luminaires closest to the window walls should be controlled separately so that it may be switched or dimmed when there is sufficient daylight

findings.antecedent: Multi-lamp luminaires tandem-wired with adjacent luminaires (for 'step dimming')
findings.quote: This 'step dimming' avoids the increased cost of dimming ballasts (currently about 50% higher than on/off ballasts)

findings.antecedent: Automatic dimming of fluorescent lighting systems in response to daylight (current technology)
findings.consequent: Widespread implementation, lamp life, ballast reliability, commissioning difficulty of photosensors
findings.quote: Automatic dimming of fluorescent lighting systems in response to daylight faces several technological and social barriers to widespread implementation. Incompatibility of certain dimming ballasts with certain lamps have led to shortened lamp life and reduced confidence of lighting system specifiers in dimming systems. The major lamp manufacturers are working to develop lamp/ballast systems that promise improved lamp and ballast reliability. Photosensors... have been difficult to commission and are the weak link in saving energy in an automatically controlled daylight system [20].

findings.antecedent: Self-commissioning photosensor technology
findings.quote: The recent development of a self-commissioning photosensor technology offers hope for improved daylight dimming systems.

synthesis_conclusions: Daylighting creates interesting, dynamic interiors that support human health and activities while reducing energy demand.
Daylighting provides economic benefits through energy savings (lighting, cooling, peak load reduction) and improved occupant productivity, job satisfaction, and reduced absenteeism.
Daylight influences human photobiological systems, potentially leading to increased alertness, better sleep, and improved performance by triggering circadian systems.
Effective daylighting requires careful architectural design (building configuration, fenestration, sun control, interior surfaces) and appropriate lighting controls.
Improper daylighting design can lead to discomfort, vision impairment, and excessive energy use.
evidence_gaps: Quantification of daylighting's impact on people.
Enhancing building designs and technologies to respond better to human preferences and needs.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Strategic integration of daylighting reduces electrical energy consumption for artificial lighting and can influence thermal loads in buildings.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Impact of Light on Human Physiology and Psychology
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to appropriate natural light patterns positively influences human circadian rhythms, visual comfort, mood, and cognitive performance.
